title: Introduction to OR and Models
subject: LIT 803
description: Twenty-five questions across easy, medium and hard on the history and characteristics of operations research and the types of model, with the tollbooth example.

questions.prompt: Which kind of problem does Operations Research focus on mainly?
options: Poorly structured, non-programmable problems that are complex and uncertain
Routine, programmable problems with predictable parameters
Payroll processing and automated reordering
Problems with no uncertainty and one variable
questions.explanation: Structured problems are routine and well defined. OR gives quantitative rigour to the novel, complex ones, such as expansion, capital allocation and facility relocation.

questions.prompt: Where and when did Operations Research originate?
options: In the United States during the Industrial Revolution
In Great Britain during World War II
In Germany before World War I
In Nigeria after independence
questions.explanation: The British military gathered teams of scientists, mathematicians and engineers to study military operations.

questions.prompt: Which of these was an early application of OR?
options: Designing office furniture
Setting retail prices
Optimising the deployment of radar warning systems
Planning school timetables
questions.explanation: Early work also covered air defence tactics, convoy routing and antisubmarine warfare.

questions.prompt: How is Operations Research defined in the notes?
options: A set of computer programs for storing business data
The study of past accounts to find errors
A method of hiring staff for industrial firms
The application of an updated scientific method and an interdisciplinary team approach to represent complex relationships as mathematical models
questions.explanation: Its objective is to give quantitative bases for optimal decisions and to uncover new operational problems.

questions.prompt: Which of these is one of the four essential characteristics of OR?
options: A single-discipline focus
A systems overview
A fixed one-time solution
Optimising each department separately
questions.explanation: The four are systems overview, interdisciplinary team approach, planned approach and uncovering new problems.

questions.prompt: What is sub-optimisation?
options: Departments optimising their own measures at the expense of the whole organisation
Finding the best solution for the whole firm
Using a cheaper model to save time
Solving a problem with only two variables
questions.explanation: OR aims at overall system performance, such as total firm profit, instead of local department results.

questions.prompt: What is a model, according to the notes?
options: An exact physical copy of a factory
A list of all costs in a firm
An abstract representation of reality that captures the essential cause-and-effect relationships of a system
A report written after a project ends
questions.explanation: A model leaves out unnecessary real-world complexity.

questions.prompt: Which three basic categories of model do the notes describe?
options: Static, dynamic and random
Linear, curved and flat
Simple, medium and complex
Iconic, analogue and symbolic
questions.explanation: Iconic models are physical, analogue models are diagrammatical, and symbolic models are mathematical.

questions.prompt: Which is an example of an iconic (physical) model?
options: A flowchart
A scale model airplane
A linear programming model
An inventory formula
questions.explanation: Iconic models keep the visual properties of the real object. Flowcharts are analogue and LP models are symbolic.

questions.prompt: Which is an example of an analogue (diagrammatical) model?
options: A scale model airplane
A linear programming model
A physical prototype
An electrical circuit diagram
questions.explanation: Analogue models represent behaviour with analogous properties. Other examples are flowcharts, organisational charts and maps.

questions.prompt: Which is an example of a symbolic (mathematical) model?
options: A queuing model
An architectural miniature
An organisational chart
A scale prototype
questions.explanation: Symbolic models use symbols, equations and expressions. LP models, inventory formulas and queuing models are the examples given.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between deterministic and probabilistic models?
options: Deterministic models include risk, while probabilistic models assume certainty
Deterministic models are always dynamic, while probabilistic models are always static
Deterministic models assume all parameters are known with certainty, while probabilistic models include random variables and probability distributions
There is no difference between them
questions.explanation: Probabilistic models are also called stochastic models.

questions.prompt: Which is a descriptive model?
options: A linear programming model
A model that always finds the single best solution
An objective function that is maximised
A queuing model
questions.explanation: Descriptive models, such as simulation and queuing, show how a system behaves. Optimising models, such as LP, find the best choice.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between static and dynamic models?
options: Static models look at a system at one point in time, while dynamic models treat time as a variable and account for change
Static models include time, while dynamic models ignore it
Static models are numerical, while dynamic models are not
Static models always use simulation
questions.explanation: Dynamic models are continuous or multi-stage over time.

questions.prompt: When is a simulation model used instead of a direct analytical one?
options: When all the data are known exactly
When closed-form solutions are mathematically intractable
When only one variable exists
When a physical prototype is cheaper
questions.explanation: Simulation models step through the operating rules over simulated time to approximate behaviour.

questions.prompt: In the general model E = f(X₁, …, Xₙ; Y₁, …, Yₘ), what are the Yⱼ?
options: Controllable variables such as production quantities
The measure of overall effectiveness
Uncontrollable variables set by external forces, such as raw material costs, demand and weather
The functional relationship between variables
questions.explanation: E is the effectiveness measure, the Xᵢ are controllable, the Yⱼ are uncontrollable, and f links them.

questions.prompt: What does the paint manufacturer example show?
options: OR studies never find new problems
A study of warehouse stock levels may reveal blending scheduling bottlenecks at the roller mills
Warehouse studies always lower stock
Roller mills should be closed
questions.explanation: This is the fourth characteristic: OR often uncovers new problems for study.

questions.prompt: In the tollbooth example, which pairing is correct?
options: E: number of toll lanes open; X: driver wait time; Y: hourly arrival rate
E: hourly arrival rate; X: weather; Y: number of lanes open
E: weather conditions; X: arrival rate; Y: number of collectors
E: driver wait time plus operating cost; X: number of toll lanes open; Y: hourly arrival rate of vehicles
questions.explanation: The measure of effectiveness is minimised, the controllable factors are lanes, collectors and electronic passes, and the uncontrollable factors are arrivals, weather and exact-change payers.

questions.prompt: Which relationships link arrival rate, service rate and the number of lanes to queue length in the tollbooth example?
options: Queuing system equations
Linear programming constraints
The EOQ formula
A transportation tableau
questions.explanation: They are used to compute expected queue length (Lq) and delay time (Wq).

questions.prompt: Which set of questions must every general OR formulation answer?
options: Cost, time, quality and risk
Who, what, when and where
The measure of effectiveness, the controllable factors, the uncontrollable factors and the functional relationships
The objective, the constraints, the algorithm and the software
questions.explanation: These four questions define E, Xᵢ, Yⱼ and f.

questions.prompt: A production department builds large stocks to cut its own costs, but this raises the firm's warehouse costs. Which OR idea does this break?
options: Systems overview, because it is sub-optimisation
Interdisciplinary teamwork
The planned approach
Uncovering new problems
questions.explanation: OR seeks the best result for the whole system, not for one department.

questions.prompt: A study team of mathematicians, cost accountants and behavioural experts reflects which OR characteristic?
options: The systems overview
The interdisciplinary (mixed) team approach
Uncovering new problems
Use of iconic models
questions.explanation: No single discipline has all the skills needed for multifaceted problems.

questions.prompt: Why do OR models need periodic review?
options: Models become more accurate with age
Reviews remove the need for data
Models are only valid for one day
Operating conditions change continuously, so models must be updated to stay valid
questions.explanation: This is part of the fourth characteristic.

questions.prompt: Which sequence starts the planned approach (updated scientific method) correctly?
options: Build the model, observe the environment, implement, define the problem
Implement, validate, observe, define the problem
Observe the environment, define the problem and objectives, build mathematical models, evaluate alternatives
Select the optimal solution, build the model, define the problem, observe
questions.explanation: The later steps are selecting the optimum, experimentation and validation, implementation with controls, and using computers.

questions.prompt: Which pairing of model classification and example is correct?
options: Descriptive: linear programming; optimising: simulation
Descriptive: simulation; optimising: linear programming
Descriptive: EOQ; optimising: queuing
Descriptive: Simplex; optimising: queuing
questions.explanation: Descriptive models do not pick the best option, while optimising models find the best solution for an objective function.
